utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I have to inform this esteemed Court about certain points that need to be clear. There is a huge difference between reports and information. Everyone knows what a report must contain. Pieces of information is something of an entirely different nature. If Mr. Seselj ran into me at the Crisis Staff, then he would ask me, Rankic, is there anything new on the ground? Quite logically, I would tell him whatever news I had, but that's no report. A report is an official document that has to contain a number of elements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The English term used is "reports" in paragraph 32. In your language, how do you say "information" in your language, and how do you call a report in your language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Information" is "informacija." "Report," in the military sense, is "raport." And "report" is "izvestaj."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, "raport" is used in Serbian only in the military terminology.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is this, therefore, an outright lie, and that I didn't give -- sorry, when you said I didn't give any instructions on how to treat women, children, civilians, prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time the Crisis Staff was set up, you gave us information. And when the War Staff was set up, you told us exactly what to convey to the volunteers on how to conduct themselves on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, sir. To demonstrate that Mr. Seselj has a fair trial and that he is entitled to a trial according to the Rules, I must state that in the B/C/S statement you have signed, it is the term "information" which has been used in your language. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a witness who perjured himself in the courtroom and who claimed that every time I came to the headquarters of the Serbian Radical Party, in the morning the entire War Staff lined up and that the chief or his deputy gave me a military report and marched through the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only laugh at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Would that be a sign of yes or no, that it's not true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did Ljubisa Petkovic, who's your neighbour -- and he's now an MP of the Serbian Radical Party, who had also been interrogated by OTP investigators. He gave a certain statement, and as far as I know he didn't say anything untruthful in that statement, but he acted as a hero and refused to testify before The Hague Tribunal, even at the cost of a prison term. The Serbian Radical Party appreciates that a lot, and he showed Borislav Jovic, Aleksandar Vasiljevic, and many other Serbs what a real hero is, because they testified, and he didn't. Is it true that my first submission as my special defence was on 400 pages quoting from my speeches and public appearances where I stated what humane treatment of prisoners of war, women, children, civilians, should be; that the enemy is an enemy only as long as he carries weapons on the front-line. At the moment he lays down his arms, he has to be treated humanely? Was that my standard language at every opportunity?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and we said the same. In your absence, we were duty-bound to convey the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And there is television footage testifying to those speeches?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And TV crews were present when volunteers were sent off.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How about your statement in paragraph 28? You say I said: "Be heroes, kill the Ustashas, fight for a Greater Serbia." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you really say, as it states in this paragraph, that I'm a lunatic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you say I was a fool in one of the later statements that was corrected?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You never said that, and they included it in your statement against your will?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many things, not only that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did we ever send a criminal as our own volunteer while knowing that he was bent on crime?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never sent anyone who was a known criminal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know of a single case where a volunteer of ours committed serious criminal offences on the front-line?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any such case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It says here that you stated that there were a certain number of volunteers who were possibly mental patients even before they became volunteers. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can't be true, because all volunteers had to produce their military service books to the Serbian Radical Party headquarters, and if anyone had been mentally disturbed, it would have been written in their service books.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And in paragraph 30, it says there was a case of a volunteer who had killed five or six prisoners. His nickname was Topola. Did you say that, that Topola was one of our volunteers?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that. I don't even know who that Topola man is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, it says here that you drove Topola from the front-line to Vukovar after that incident, and after the killings, back to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the first I hear of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You have no idea how this found its way into your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No clue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you perhaps find out later? Because the first witness here was Goran Stoparic, who has testified that Topola was a member of the Leva Supoderica Unit, but already in October 1991 he was expelled for lack of discipline.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have a chance of knowing all the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party. There were thousands of them. I knew certain commanders whom I was in touch with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He said not that he was our volunteer, but just a volunteer, because Leva Supoderica did not contain exclusively SRS volunteers.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did a single volunteer of the SRS, at the cost of his life, ever accept to wear a red five-pointed star on his cap?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We saw a photograph of Topola here wearing a white belt of the military police and five-pointed red star on his cap. He was recognised by a general who was sent by Aleksandar Vasiljevic to Vukovar to do the execution of the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we need to show this photograph to the witness again? If there's no need, we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It also says here that towards the end of November, after the fall of Vukovar, Milan Lancuzanin, also known as Kameni, came with Katic to Belgrade to describe the circumstances under which Topola allegedly removed five or six Croatian prisoners from the collection centre in Velepromet, and there was information available that these men had been killed. And after that - that's paragraph 31 - you went to Vukovar to pick up Topola and get him back to Serbia. Is this at all possible?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Milan Lancuzanin and Slobodan Katic came to Belgrade more than once. I can't remember on what business. Of course, I spoke to them, but Topola was never a subject of our conversations. When I went to Vukovar, the fighting was over. There was no longer any need for volunteers in Vukovar, and we wanted to relocate them to Western Slavonia, where they were needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did the volunteers go back as soon as Vukovar fell?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The volunteers of the SRS, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On the 18th, 19th, 20th November, were they already returning?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it true that Slobodan Katic remained to live in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and he married there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did Little Joe stay in Vukovar to live?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know anyone else who stayed in Vukovar to live? There's several more cases.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of anyone but these two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it true what it says in paragraph 30, that I, allegedly, finding out that Topola had committed this crime, stated, when asked what are we to do, What can I do now? Disarm the man and get him back home. He's tired. Could I have said that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you say this to the investigators of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, those are certainly not my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: This is repeated through all of the five statements. Did you ever see it in that statement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never read any of my statements, and therefore I don't accept them as mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When these corrections were made, did you make these corrections while reading, or did they re-tell you the statement, or did they read back to you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They read back to me from the laptop all my statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It says here that in paragraph 31 you described Topola; that he was huge, dark-skinned, dark brown hair, over six feet tall, huge hands, that he had a long beard, and he was in his mid 30s. You don't know whether he was a member of the SRS, but he was certainly a member of the Serbian Chetnik Movement; is that your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We have been shown here a photograph of Topola. He really did have a beard, but it was a very neat, small beard, trimmed. He was very neatly dressed, and he had the insignia of a military policeman. Where he got them, nobody could explain. But you have never seen him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Registry prepare this photograph. It is an exhibit, and I'd like to show it to the witness. It was shown when that protected witness was testifying, if you remember, the retired officer who recognised Topola.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While the Registrar is bringing up the photograph: Witness, the case put forward by the Prosecutor runs as follows - this is contained in the indictment and in the pre-trial brief - is that Seselj was made aware of crimes that had been committed by volunteers; namely, volunteers from the Serbian Radical Party. In paragraph 39 of your statement, which has been signed by you in your language, you say that: "Mr. Seselj was made aware of the crimes committed by Topola, and he said, himself, 'Well, what can I do now? Disarm him, send him home. He's tired.'" This is incriminating evidence against Mr. Seselj, and this has been signed by you. You have been asked a lot of questions. Ms. Biersay has put questions to you, Mr. Seselj is putting questions to you, and I'm putting questions to you also. You signed a whole series of statements and incriminating evidence. Can you tell us why you signed these after having, as is normal, read the statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm really glad that you have now put the right question to me, why I signed what I signed. From day 1, and from my first contact with the OTP, huge pressure was put on me. I was even threatened that I would be sent to Bosnia. And they told me that I was not a sweet-smelling flower and that I was involved in some war crimes in Bosnia, although I don't know. I was never involved in anything. If I had been, I would have already been on trial for any such thing. But I didn't know what my rights were. I now know that I did not have to provide any statements to the OTP, but I didn't know it at the time. They put pressure on me, and I was afraid, like any other normal person would have been. Can you imagine if somebody threatened you to be -- that you will be sent to Bosnia, they would provide two witnesses who would perjure themselves, and you would end up in prison for 20 years? How would you behave in my place? I did not read anything. I was not even interested in what it says in any of the statements. I was just glad to be out of there. They'd write whatever they wanted to write, I signed whatever they asked me to sign, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: With respect to clarification, I read "they would provide two witnesses who would perjure themselves." Is the witness telling the Court that the OTP representative said that they would have two witnesses perjure themselves in order to incriminate him? I don't fully understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you know, I'm quite used to carrying out some investigations, and so I'm listening to what Ms. Biersay is saying, I'm listening to Mr. Seselj, and I'm listening to you. What I would like to know is the following: When the investigator from the OTP threatened to start an investigation against you in Bosnia, did he say that there would be witnesses that would support their case? Is that what you were trying to say here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, yes -- no, they didn't tell me that they would bring two witnesses who would perjure themselves; no, far from that. It was just my way of thinking, that they could do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you're drawing your own conclusion. It's not the investigator who said that. Mr. Seselj, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The OTP disclosed to me your resignation that you signed on the 12th of December, 1991, and in which it reads: "Because of the total confusion and lack of organisation in the work of the War Staff of the SRS, as well as in the entire party, I hereby resign as the deputy chief of the War Staff of the SRS." Did you sign this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That was on the 12th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And what was the immediate reason? Did you perhaps have an argument with Ljubisa Petkovic before that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a minor argument with him, but that was not the reason for my resignation. I had some family problems. I had neglected my family. The conditions of life were hard. I had two young children. I wanted to make sure that my resignation would be accepted, and I had to fabricate a very strong reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And that's why you entered into all those arguments with the War Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you ever talk to me about your resignation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you ever work in the War Staff after you submitted your resignation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it true that Zoran Drazilovic, immediately after your resignation, became the deputy chief of the War Staff, and the chief at the time was Ljubisa Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I have a statement to that effect by Ljubisa Petkovic and Zoran Drazilovic, and that is that he immediately took over from you. Did you -- after that, did you ever take volunteers anywhere?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you ever get in contact with anybody on behalf of the SRS, and especially with regard to the deployment of volunteers, once you resigned?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And it says here that you took SRS volunteers to Zvornik at the beginning of April 1992. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact that I no longer had any duties in the War Staff of the SRS speaks to the contrary. I was not duty-bound, and nobody could issue an order for me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it true that you went to Zvornik with Zuco, Zuco's brother, and Miroslav Bogdanovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Zuco from 1991 while he was a volunteer in East Slavonia, and I also know Miki Bogdanovic, who was a member of the War Staff, but I never went to Zvornik with them. I went on one occasion to Mali Zvornik, but I had some private business there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you hail from Bogatic, which is close to Zvornik, on the Drina?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Not far from the Drina, yeah. And can you remember for how long did Zuca remain a member of the SRS in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the date, but I know that he was excluded from the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We also have his statement provided to the Court, that he left the SRS sometime in September. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you ever hear -- actually, Zuca stated before the judiciary bodies of Serbia that you came to Zvornik together with him. However, he wanted to cover up the true situation, and he mentioned your name instead of the name of Milorad Vukovic. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard from unofficial sources, but I don't know how important it is to mention hearsay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All sorts of hearsay is used here. Did you hear that immediately on the eve of war in Zvornik, Zuco came there, together with his brother, Milorad Ulemek, Legija, who was later known as Lukovic, and Miroslav Bogdanovic, and that they came across a Muslim check-point and that they were arrested by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear that, because I still had friends who were members of the SRS, irrespective of the fact that I no longer had any position there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What would have been the reason for them to change all that, and then we see a similar thing in your statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you told us that you resigned in December 1991, which means that you should no longer have anything to do with the movement and with the Serbian Radical Party. But, strangely enough, in paragraph 101 of your statement, in your own language, you say that in April 1992, with five members of the SRS, including yourself, you went to Zvornik. So this is where I don't really understand things anymore, and perhaps the investigator did not pick up on this discrepancy or contradiction. You're saying, under oath, that you never went to Zvornik in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in Mali Zvornik towards the end of April 1992, just passing through it, and I did come across some people whom I know. I sat down with them in Jezero Hotel. We shared a drink and chatted about the situation in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that all very well, but in paragraph 101, it says: "At the end of April 1992, we went to Zvornik, myself included, to discuss the issue of sending volunteers." So you were saying that you were still active there. But now you say that you went there, but you went there as a tourist, which means that you did not take part in any discussions as a member of the SRS party.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In April 1992, I did not have any competencies with regard to the War Staff of the Serbian Radical Party, which means that I did not have any power to talk to anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] [previous translation continues] ... to complete, because then I will give the floor to Mr. Seselj. But in paragraph 102, you say that you met with the municipal authorities at the Jezero Hotel in Mali Zvornik, and among them there was Pazin, there was Pavlovic, and so on and so forth. So when you read this, you have the feeling that you really are at the heart of things. And then you sign this statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I met with some people in Mali Zvornik, and Mali Zvornik is on the Serbian side of the Drina and not on the Bosnian side of the Drina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, did you receive the English translation of Mr. Rankic's resignation letter? It should be in the binder. I can provide you with that in the Serbian language, the original. Okay, you have it; fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And now it says here, in paragraph 32 of the first statement, that: "One group of our volunteers, under the command of Goran Vuckovic, aka Zuca, commander of the Yellow Wasps, does not recognise any command ." And that was alledgedly towards the end of May 1991. Did you ever hear of volunteers of the SRS having withdrawn as soon as Kula Grad had fallen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, before you answer the question, I don't want to take you by surprise. You are challenging some facts that are very clear, where other people were there. I'm going to quote three of them: Zoran Pazin, Brano Grujic, and Marko Pavlovic. Brano Grujic. I don't know if they're still alive, I don't know if they're dead, but in this case at hand the OTP could, as early as tomorrow, send someone there to meet with those two or three people, and they could ask them, Have you met with this witness? And they could say, Of course we met with him, because we had a meeting at the hotel on such and such topic. And then it would show that you lied. And in the same line, Mr. Seselj, with his associates, could actually gather the testimony of those various people, and they could confirm that they have never seen you and that you never had a discussion with them. So you're aware of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am absolutely aware of everything that I am saying, and I am telling you I did meet with those people towards the end of April. I can't remember the exact date, of course. It was a long time ago. We met in the Jezero Hotel, on the Serbian side, not on the Bosnian side. It was in Mali Zvornik. We shared a drink, we chatted. It was all informal. And then I proceeded to tend to my own private business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's in the transcript. Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've forgotten my question in the meantime. You interrupt me so often that I forget what I want to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The question, I believe, was that all the volunteers of the SRS, immediately upon the fall of Kula Grad, returned to Belgrade; do you know that? And that was on the 26th of April, I believe.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that for a fact. I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And now Zuca, could he, between 6 and 26 of April, be in command of any unit in the territory of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Repeat the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Between the 6th and the 26th of April.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On the 7th of April, the Muslims captured him. Then he was released, because the Serbs had promised that they would release Fadil Mujic and let him travel abroad via Serbia. It was a barter deal. And then he got involved in the fighting for Kula Grad. According to what I know, he did not have a command function.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the same what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that Igor Markovic Detachment was set up after the fall of Kula Grad?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that only later when I read it in the Serbian newspapers, when Zuco's group was arrested, if you remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Zuco's group was arrested sometime the beginning of July. It doesn't really matter. The Igor Markovic Detachment was established, and then later on it was called the Yellow Wasps. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that from other people's stories.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I have Zuco's statement proving that, and all the other indicators prove that. And you know that in Belgrade a group of people were on trial, they were charged with committing crimes in Zvornik. Among the accused, there were also Brano Grujic and Marko Pavlovic or, rather, Popovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Branko.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, Branko Popovic. And that their proceedings were separated from the rest of the group, and it doesn't say anywhere in the court documents that Branko Popovic or Marko Pavlovic had used to work for the State Security. And in paragraph 35 of your statement, it says that he was a member of the State Security and that you stated that. Did you state that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How would I be able to know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Allegedly this was told to you by Vlada Slon form Loznica.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know people tend to say all sorts of things. I really don't know what he was, what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In paragraph 34, it says that I denied that that group contained SRS volunteers and that they were headed by Zuco, and that you protested against that. If you remember, I supported the arrest of Zuco's group, Pivarski's group, and Niska's group, and that arrest was carried out by the special police of Republika Srpska. Did do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that all the groups that didn't recognise the VRS and they didn't want to be placed under their command, you wanted -- you asked for their arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In one of the groups, there was also a volunteer of SRS. He went there of his own will, and you can see in the court documents that he was first a volunteer of the SRS and then he joined the Zuco groups. The Trial Chamber is in the possession of that sentence to the Zvornik group. However, here in paragraph 34, it says that you and I confronted with this regard and that you protested about the fact that I supported the arrest of that group, because you personally had taken there [as interpreted]. Did you state that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never stated that. And, second of all, how could I have confronted you or protested against what you did? At the time, I didn't have any position in the SRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It says here that: "This was the highest point of my conflict with Seselj, and that conflict started when he became closer to Milosevic and gave up on the ideas of monarchy." First of all, did I ever support any monarchy and the idea of monarchy?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What do you think?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not for me to think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: A normal person who purports to be clever and intelligent and educated, could such a person be a monarchist? There are states like Denmark which still cherish that tradition. They have not been able to get rid of the king, but they did have a crazy king, Edward VII, and owing to him and his lack of interference with politics, Denmark is now a democratic state. And there are also other states who have gotten rid of their monarchies as a relic of the past.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are also crazy presidents, not only monarchs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yeah, but you can remove the president. And the monarch, when he goes crazy, the only thing you can do is to kill him. You can't remove a monarchy in a constitutional way. Very well. Did I ever become close to Milosevic, do you think? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, only after the war, if I remember it well, in 1997, on the eve of NATO bombing, a government of national salvation was set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It was in 1998, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I misspoke. It was the Government of National Unity. That's what we call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And it says that after that, you resigned your position as deputy chief of the War Staff and left the Serbian Chetnik Movement. So you resigned only after Zuco was arrested and after I supported that arrest, the arrest of Zuco and Miski [phoen], and Stojan Pivarski. And that make it August 1992. But we have a document, signed in your hand, that you resigned on 12th December, 1991, eight months earlier. Is it absolutely untrue, the paragraph 34?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document is self-explanatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you responsible for this untruth or the OTP?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't write it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Then it says that I ordered that Zuco's group should be transferred to Skelani. Half of them agreed, the other half didn't, so they committed crimes. Is it even remotely the truth?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could I know what was going on there if I held no position and no duties?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, they put it in your statement.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could have put there anything they liked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: This is repeated throughout the five statements.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you it's their statement, not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then in paragraph 35, it says: "Seselj never ordered me to bring this group back to Serbia. He simply ordered me to move them to another location in Bosnia. That I was informed about the conduct of these people, but did nothing to prevent them from committing crimes." And that you confirmed that the Vuckovic brothers left Serbia as SRS volunteers.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how would you be able to order me anything at that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, it's in your statement.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying again, it's not my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm saying to the Serbian public that they should stigmatise this conduct of the Prosecution. Did you sign this statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: It's not an opportunity for him to preach anything to the Serbian public. He's already stigmatised Serbs who are willing to come and testify before this Tribunal, and it's really outrageous that he continues to do this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I'm defending myself here partly because I can do so in public to some extent. If this trial were entirely in closed session, I would not represent myself at all, because publicity is my only protection. Between the Trial Chamber, who can't wait to take my head off, and the Prosecution, who only want it -- who only want the same. I have no one here, no legal assistants, no case managers, no lawyers. I have no one here; I'm alone. And I hope that you will deduct from Ms. Biersay the 14 seconds she abused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, it's very simple. There are statements invoking Mr. Seselj's liability on a whole series of events. There is a statement that you signed, personally, confirming the previous statements. So your position is the following: You said that you signed because you were threatened of being tried in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so you decided to sign everything that was shown to you. Mr. Seselj, paragraph by paragraph, is making you say the opposite of what is written in those statements, statements which you signed, and it could last quite a while because we are still to cover quite a few paragraphs. So I'm going to put the question to you once again. You are saying today under oath, under oath, the truth and only the truth, and you're stating that the previous statements have been made because you were under duress?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you claim also what's written in paragraph 35 is also not true -- shall I go on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, my colleagues and I are wondering whether it's any use of you continuing on this line of questioning, because every time he will say, This is not what I said. So I'm just asking this question --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know in advance, Mr. President. What other line should I take? Why don't you tell me in advance which line of questioning suits you best? I'm using the line of questioning that is the most successful for me. Do you think I'm going to pick up on what Ms. Biersay did and follow that? No, I'm not going to. I'm interested in facts. I want to know -- I want the public to know what exactly the truth is, what the facts are. I am --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. You were given two hours. Please proceed, and take your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you also say that paragraph 35 is untrue as well?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, paragraph 38: "The commander of TO Borovo Selo was late Vukasin Soskocanin, who was shot in the back and killed in mid-May 1991." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were the rumours. I don't know if it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Then how come it's in your statement? As far as I know, he drowned in the Danube River, crossing it by boat, because there was no other way the locals of Borovo Selo could communicate with Serbia.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is just blah-blah-blah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, he couldn't swim, and he was -- he drowned?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm saying that he was shot in the back. That's "blah-blah-blah."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It's in your statement.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Soskocanin met with Seselj when the latter visited Borovo Selo. I did meet with him several times. I agreed with him that the first volunteers of the SRS, in end April 1991, should be sent to Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about one meeting, and I was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In paragraph 39, it says that you stated, allegedly: "I personally think that the incident in Borovo Selo, when, on the 2nd of May, 1991, 12 Croatian MUP members got killed, was orchestrated by the State Security Service of Serbia. Seselj was not so powerful at that time. His power grew only later." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only know what I say. The units of the MUP raided the center of Borovo Selo and attacked the local commune when the agreement to remove barricades had already been reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Which MUP?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatian, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What would the State Security Service of Serbia then have to do with the incident in Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe they met the MUP of Croatia and got confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It says the incident was orchestrated by the SDB, the State Security Service of Serbia. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That there was 16 volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party there and one volunteer of the Serbian Popular Renewal.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was killed at the entrance to the town hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And he wasn't fighting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was reading a newspaper there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I went to attend his funeral.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So did I.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And when the Croatian police raided, our volunteers fought back, and then the JNA came in to save the Croatian policemen. They separated the two sides and helped the Croatians get out.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, the JNA was playing UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is this a well-known fact to the Serbian public? How does the State Security Service of Serbia come in?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Here in paragraph 40, you allegedly described how Milic was killed, that he was not armed, and you say: "Seselj is a bit of an exhibitionist and he likes to brag about things that he never did. That's why he said the Borovo Selo operation was carried out by his volunteers. Seselj would do anything to be at the center of attention."

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, how come it's written like that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ask the Prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did 16 volunteers of the SRS fight with Croatian police in Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, led by Mladen Tersijevic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But this Mladen wasn't even involved in the fighting, because he happened to be without a weapon, but his deputy, Oliver Barrett, took up his duties and made sure that the locals get involved in the fighting.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But the first to fight back were the volunteers of the SRS. Is that what you would call bragging?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how they qualified it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: First I brag about military successes, and then I'm a war criminal. And then in paragraph 48, it says that somebody very powerful in the government was behind this Pekic, the president of the Association of Serbs Outside Serbia. First of all, he wasn't the president; he was a member of the board.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was a national hero?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was a partisan general from second -- World War II?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was he a president or a high official of the Association of War Veterans?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did he have enough -- didn't he have enough authority that he had to find someone in the army to whom he would say, Don't destroy these weapons, I'll take them on?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Were there other such generals? Have you heard of Radojica Penezic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He also got involved, and many others, but Pekic played the most prominent role. And it says here that Milosevic's regime was against Chetniks, and that's absolutely true, but he was very happy at the first opportunity to send volunteers to the front-line in order to get rid of them. Is that true? Did Milosevic's regime send any volunteers at all?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It all went bypassing Milosevic and his regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did we handle the sending of volunteers until October 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did they cross the river by boats because the police was guarding the bridges?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I was with them several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did we clash with them several times, with the police, because they would intercept these people who were not carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 44, you say: "We got some premises in Lipovac." I don't remember anything like that. There were premises for the Assembly of all volunteers, not specifically ours.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the assembly centre for all volunteers before they were sent on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And it says the buses were provided by the Ministry for Relations with Serbs Outside Serbia. If that were true, the Prosecution would have found the necessary documentation in his ministry and brought it here, right? Because you can't get any buses without travel documents.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: If a company from Serbia, as a sponsor, provides the buses, then they can be used.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Can a driver get out of Serbia in a company vehicle without a travel order?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 45, it says when you arrived with a group of volunteers to Vukovar -- you went to Vukovar; I don't think it's in dispute.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: This document by Ljubisa Petkovic, together with the list of names of volunteers, was given to Milan Lancuzanin, also known as Kameni.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then it says: " ... also to Stanko Vujanovic and to Stanko's wife, Nada, who was the secretary of the TO." Did you have three lists?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had one list in duplicate, but one copy I had to keep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you gave the list only to Kameni?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He had to get one copy, and I had to return one copy to the War Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Where do Stanko Vujanovic and his wife come in?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I said they were present when I gave the list to Kameni.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The headquarters of the Leva Supoderica Unit, was it in Kameni's house?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in Nova Street. I don't know whose house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember Stanko Vujanovic had his own unit under the command of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: Could we slow down, please. None of the speakers have really slowed down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj and Mr. Witness, again, please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In paragraph 47, it says that the commander of the Sector South was Mile Mrksic. Fine. Veselin Sljivancanin was the operative officer of the sector in charge of the TO. Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know what Sljivancanin was at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know he was a major.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was he a security officer of the Guards Brigade and then security officer of the Operative Group South?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How can he be the operative group officer of the sector? Did the security officer have any command over units?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who could be subordinate to him? Only the military police; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Not always, though, but only on the orders of the commander or along the security line.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did security officers have two lines of command; they were subordinate to commanders of their unit, and they were subordinate to the Security Service of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We're still on the first statement. You say: "Mid-November, before the fall of Vukovar, I went to Vukovar." That was in the first half of November. We also have here the exact date in the transcripts; that you were there, that "a group of volunteers went with me." Is that true, when I went from Belgrade to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. A group of volunteers joined you in Sid. They were to be the escorts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They met me in Sid?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know I was driving my personal car, a Toyota Corolla, and there was my -- there was Petar Panic with me?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, your personal bodyguard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And it also says here that from Lipovaca, I went to Vukovar on an armoured personnel carrier provided by the JNA. They gave us four APCs. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember what the escort was, but there was some buses carrying other volunteers going the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Please, we're talking about military APCs. It was, in fact, a combat armoured vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have had one hour already, and you have one hour left. In 15 minutes, we will have a break, around a quarter to 6.00. We will have a 15-minute break then and resume at 6.00. Mr. Seselj will resume. We will see at what point he will stop and let Ms. Biersay put her questions. Given that we are running late, we will have to go beyond 7.00 p.m., because we must finish this witness today. We should finish around 20 minutes past 7.00 or 25 minutes past 7.00. I just wanted all and everyone to be informed. Please proceed, Mr. Seselj. You have a quarter of an hour before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I first went to Mirkovci, near Vinkovci, and then to Vukovar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the sequence, but it is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In one part of that journey from Sid to Mirkovci, the Ustashi threatened the traffic, and that's why I had to use the APC. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the place was called Siska Planica [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And when I returned from Mirkovci, I continued in my own vehicle to Vukovar because there was no danger between Sid and Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: A witness perjured himself here. He said he was a volunteer. He said that he fought from Sid to Vukovar, trying to liberate the Serbian villages around there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. The characterisation of any statement made in this courtroom as perjury is only for this Trial Chamber and not for Mr. Seselj to cast aspersions to other witnesses about past testimony. So we object to him using this repeatedly when he discusses past evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is my right to qualify anybody's testimony. And when a witness perjures himself, I shall say so. I didn't say that the witness is a liar; I just said that he perjured him. And it is indeed a perjury that he fought from and Sid to Vukovar. There was no fighting there ever. Those villages were free and liberated from day one. And when there was fighting for Vukovar, Serbs had already had part of Vukovar under control, because they had resided as a majority population. My main thesis is that all charges against me are based on witnesses who have perjured themselves. The whole process is just a fabrication; it's a political process, and I blame Carla Del Ponte for that. You cannot change my thesis at your own will. And the fact that this is not happening in other proceedings, you have to thank the lawyers for that. They sacrificed their interest for the big bucks that they receive for their work. And now what we have in England, General Krstic almost -- was almost slaughtered in prison. He was sentenced to 35 years, and still he had nothing whatsoever to do with crimes. And now, instead of informing the media that General Krstic was slaughtered by Bosnian Muslims and Albanian Muslims who are criminals, there is false information in the media that he had been beaten up, which is nonsense. You cannot -- but the truth will out. You cannot prevent the media from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please get back to the statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And now we are on the way to Vukovar, and I stop in Negoslavci. And there I met the then colonel, and later on General Mile Mrksic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Veselin Sljivancanin wasn't there, and Miroslav [as interpreted] Radic wasn't there, and in paragraph 53 it says that they were there. How come?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It says that I greeted them and that our exchange lasted for five minutes. I only met with Mrksic. We greeted each other, and then I proceeded towards Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, Colonel Mrksic was there, and Lieutenant-Colonel Panic was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Miodrag Panic, the chief of staff, who was later promoted into the rank of general.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the first time I was in Vukovar, I had a very small helmet, and the officers laughed at that helmet, and Miodrag Panic gave me his own helmet; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Were you there?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there you go.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And now in paragraph 54: "As we went on towards Vukovar, Sljivancanin was at the head of that convoy. We went straight into Nova Street, where Lancuzanin's headquarters was."

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing that's correct here is that the command was in that street.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I was escorted to the front-line by Major Borivoje Tesic. Have you ever heard of him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was he the commander of the 1st Assault Detachment?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And I met Sljivancanin only briefly. He was carrying a Motorola in his hand, and he was yelling or shouted back at the Ustasha Commander Jastreb?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they communicated regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I just shook his hand and I went to the front-line. I don't know whether Sljivancanin had ever been to the front-line.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was not in command of any of the units; he was a security officer, was he not? Do you agree that this is another blatant lie?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Again, it says here when we arrived in the Nova Street where Lancuzanin's command was, we were met by Minister Lancuzanin, Stanko and his wife. Do you know that I never met Miroslav Ljubovic [as interpreted] my whole life? Did you ever see us meet?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did meet him, and I don't know whether you did or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Miroljub Vujovic provided an interview to The Hague OTP. I disclosed -- I was disclosed that interview, and he confirmed there that he had never met him. I did meet Stanko. Stanko later, in 1993, became a member of the Serbian Radical Party of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and then he was elected as an MP there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As for Miroljub Vujovic, I never met him in my whole life. And it says here as well that Sljivancanin explained the situation on the front-line to me --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, but I am not aware whether or not the person whose interview the accused just referred to might be a protected witness or whether or not it's a witness who hasn't testified yet. So I would like to request that the name be redacted, or we redact, on this page, page 80 in the transcript, the question that begins at line 11.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm better informed than Mr. Marcussen. Miroljub Vujovic was never a witness here in The Hague. He was interviewed as a suspect, and then he was on trial in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In that case --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And he was tried in open trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In that case, I would request -- I would certainly maintain that we should redact this part so we don't reveal the identity of people who have been interviewed by the OTP to the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, if Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This cannot be redacted. I did not receive that as a confidential document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Seselj. If this person Miroljub Vujovic has never been the subject of a decision or has never been granted protective measures, I don't see why we would redact this, all the more so that he has tried and convicted, and his name is in the public domain. So why would you want to redact it from the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It is our submission that it is not in the public interest that people who provide information and are being interviewed by the OTP see their identity published. This is disclosure material that has best been provided to the accused for the purpose of the preparation of his case, and people should be able to speak to the Office of the Prosecutor knowing that their identity is only revealed if they become witnesses. Now, I'm also not in a position to verify whether or not there might be some protective measures with respect to this, which is why I request that we redact any -- if the Court finds later on that we un-redact, then maybe we can do that. But once the information goes out, we cannot put the cat, if I may say so, back into the bag. So as a temporary measure, I request that we redact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall confer with my colleagues and see what the position of the Chamber is on this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Protective measures cannot be applied retroactively. That man appeared in open court in Belgrade. He was on trial there. I am not going to deal with the "hows" of that trial. I just quoted one sentence from his interview, in which he said that he never met me, and he provided that statement back in 2002 or 2003, and there is nothing that can either help him or go against him in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Seselj. We are deliberating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, could you check, please, whether a decision has granted him protective measures? You can let us know after the break. But if no decision has been taken to grant him protective measures, I don't see for what reason we would redact this, all the more so that this witness had a public trial and everyone knows this individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Okay, let's go back to where we left it off. Major Borivoje Tesic, did he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a precautionary measure, we will redact between now and the break. And if you don't tell us after the break that he was granted protective measures, then this will be made public. Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who was it who explained the military situation to -- Major Borivoje Tesic or Major Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there at that moment, but I would suppose that it was Borivoje Tesic because it would have made much more sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Okay. So what it says here in paragraph 54, is it a lie or not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could not have been a security measure -- would have explained the operative situation to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that between me and Major Sljivancanin, there was always a degree of animosity, because Major Sljivancanin was in command of the guards unit that was deployed around the house of flowers when we attacked it and --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Sljivancanin was a notorious Communist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So why would he escort me to the front-line? What did we have in common?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Especially in view of the fact that I attacked his boss, Vasiljevic, in public?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In paragraph 55, it says that I said that our forces had to maintain courage and to hold on until the end. I may have said it; I don't know. It says that I wore a helmet; that's correct. Do you know why I wore a helmet? That was during my second arrival in Vukovar. The first time I arrived, the officer asked me to wear a helmet in order to exert positive influence on the young soldiers who avoided that obligation, and many lost their heads.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that that was the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And that's why I wore this helmet without a red-pointed -- five-pointed red star, in order to serve as a good example to the others.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many other regular soldiers did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that I scraped off the red star with a bayonet?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And it says here that I wore a flak-jacket. Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I never -- in my whole life, I never wore a flak-jacket, wherever I went, however dangerous it was. There are many such places in the world.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Me neither.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So why did you mention that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness and the accused please be asked to slow down and make pauses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have to ask the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And it says that Milosevic and Seselj were establishing close links. Why were you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are both going too fast. We will have our 15-minute break now and resume in 15 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I would like to thank the Trial Chamber for its understanding with respect to the protection of the individual that was discussed earlier. As far as I've been able to determine, this person has actually been a witness here, but he has testified in open session. So I think the pages that were redacted can be released. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we're going to release what we had decided to provisionally redact while waiting for your position. I also invite the witness and Mr. Seselj to slow down. Interpreters are very tired. Are you going too fast. So, Mr. Seselj, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We have arrived at paragraph 56, where it says that I, from Kameni's house, passed by the supermarket. And then from the technical school, we returned to the TO Command on foot. And in front of that command, there were several vehicles parked. That's where I stopped, and I said not a single Ustasha must leave Vukovar alive. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear such words.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So why is it in your statement, in your alleged statement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. We did invite the Ustasha to surrender, but much before you arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It says that at least 50 people were present. Is that correct? Did 50 people dare to be at one place at a moment when the Croatian artillery pounded from the center of Vukovar with mortars and from Nustar, where they had proper artillery, like cannons, Howitzers, and so on?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Howitzers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was it possible for 50 people to gather in one place for me to deliver a speech to them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But this is in your alleged statement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you several times already I don't know what it says in that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And that there were volunteers, members of the TO, and the officers of the Guards Brigade, Sljivancanin, Radic, and others. There is a slight difference between your statement from the statement of other witnesses, who said that it was in Stanko Vujanovic's house, that it was halfway between Vujanovic's house and Kameni's house, and so on and so forth. However, the tendency is present on the part of the OTP that I said that no Ustasha should be allowed to leave alive, that the guards officers were listening to that, and that's why 200 prisoners were executed in Ovcara. This is the fabrication that they put together. Do you find it funny?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you never knew that this was in your statement, the one that you signed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. And that there was general euphoria, that there was celebratory shooting in the air as a sign of support, are you aware that that is also in your alleged statement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. As far as I know, nobody normal would have spent ammunition in a situation like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And I went to the front-line, where some -- where a person could be killed at any moment. Do you know -- do you remember that a Serbian soldier died in my vicinity while I was in Vukovar? He was on a motor, he was probably a courier, and a mine exploded and killed him on the spot. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was two streets away from where you were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that I went to visit that family to express my condolences because the soldier was from Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What kind of a lunatic would gather 50 people in one place where they could be hit by a shell or a mine?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember properly, immediately after that shelling started.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When the Ustasha found out that I was in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that I remained in Vukovar and that I spent the night there in a house in Kameni's neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that Croats used agricultural planes during the night to throw boilers full of explosives on Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and gas bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that such a bullet landed very close to the house where I spent the night?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that one such bullet was thrown out, but I don't know where it exploded.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness and the accused please make pauses between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Gentlemen, you are having a private conversation, and very little of it is coming to us. So unless you speak at a pace that the interpreters are able to follow, this is all in vein. And we are not entertaining the Serbian public here in this courtroom. We are on a serious trial. So please slow down and observe a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In paragraph 60, you describe, allegedly, my departure to Western Slavonia, and you say -- I mean, allegedly you say: "I'm not 100 per cent sure, but I believe that during that tour of Western Slavonia, Zoran Drazilovic accompanied Seselj, but my bodyguard, Petar Panic, and other security men were certainly with me. And I met with volunteer commanders Radovan Novacic, Slavko Nisic, and so on." But you were not present; you just know about it. Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said was the following: As far as I know, you did visit the volunteers in Western Slavonia, and if I remember correctly, it was in November. I also went there, but those were two separate visits. I didn't go together with you. I went separately. And who accompanied you, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: To this day, you don't know how I went there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: If I tell you that I went by a JNA helicopter; that this, helicopter was secured for me by the commander of the air force, General Bozidar Stevanovic, does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know who Bozidar Stevanovic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you believe that I travelled by a JNA helicopter?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And there were two air force officers piloting the helicopter, and there was Ilija Sasic, minister of foreign affairs of the Western Slavonia region. Do you believe me?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you believe that was the way I travelled?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no reason for me not to believe you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We took the helicopter to Banja Luka, and from there, by car, to Western Slavonia. And then after touring Western Slavonia, two days later I held a rally in Banja Luka. Did you hear about that rally in the Borik Hall, where several thousands of people attended?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of that rally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear that after that, at the invitation of Milan Babic, I went -- travelled by night to Knin to prevent a mutiny organised by Captain Dragan against the legal Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was busy doing other things, but I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And at the time that Vukovar was liberated, I was still in Knin; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I remember correctly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Prosecutors have footage of my duel with Captain Dragan in Benkovac. It was shown in the courtroom. We'll not dwell on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I was wondering whether Captain Dragan is the one that has just been arrested in Australia today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's very sad news to me, Mr. President, that Captain Dragan was arrested. I was hoping they would not manage to arrest him. Despite the fact that we did not agree during the war, I cannot be happy over any extradition of Serbian fighters to the Ustasha authorities in Croatia, because they cannot have a fair trial there. Nobody can have a fair trial, including here.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could the Court please instruct him or turn his microphone off when he goes on these specific accusations that have no basis in this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed. Mr. Seselj, we are aware that Captain Dragan has been arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We've come to paragraph 63. It's about Mali Zvornik. It says: "I did not go to Seselj with Mali Zvornik after Zvornik was captured. But from what I remember, Seselj went there to hold a rally after the capture of Zvornik." Did you say this, that it was in the middle of April?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would never say that. I know that these are not my words for one simple reason: I never used the term "capture." I always spoke about liberation. Second, I persistently told the investigators that the rally of the Serbian Chetnik Movement was held in 1990, whereas they tried to convince me that it was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why would I be holding a rally in Mali Zvornik while there was still fighting in Veliki Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that would have had unfathomable consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
