utterances.text: And the volunteers had to be brought over the bridge to protect me, and they were still fighting over Kula Grad until 26th of April; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you deny that these are your words?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I deny the contents of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There's a note here of the investigator. The investigator quotes Seselj's speech from a certain paragraph of the indictment. He quotes from my alleged speech, because one false witness claimed that I held a speech in Mali Zvornik in March 1992, before the fighting in Zvornik, and that I called the Muslims "pagans," which is absolutely impossible. Have you ever heard me say anything nasty about the Islamic religion?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Had you ever heard me saying anything bad about the Catholic religion, set aside the fact that I always attacked Popes in their role as politicians, but did I ever insult the Roman Catholic religion?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Or any other religion, the Tao, the Buddhism, or any other religion?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Could a man of my educational attainment call Muslims "pagans," when Islam is a mono-theistic religion originating from the roots of Christianity and Judaism?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It's true that we had religious wars under Ottoman occupation, but that's a different matter. So you deny what's in paragraph 63. In paragraph 66 they must have asked you about Ovcara, and you said you never heard about the events there. Did we in Serbia really know what had happened in Ovcara until the exhumations began, until the Croats and the foreigners in Vukovar disclosed that there was a mass grave there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. The first time I heard of Ovcara was after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was it a closely-guarded secret kept by the Military Security Service, led by Aleksandar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must have been secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Those who organised it and those who participated in the liquidations closely guarded the secret?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And those who had command in Vukovar knew about it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Does it sound logical to you that the military commander of Vukovar comes here, after the liberation of Vukovar, to testify against me? He, the town commander where Ovcara happened, and where it was covered up, to testify against me, who didn't even know about Ovcara? Does that sound logical to you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very far from common sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Since he is a protected witness, I won't mention his name. He didn't really level any charges against me or accuse me of anything, but it's horrible that somebody who was involved is testifying against me who didn't even know about Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second, Mr. Seselj. I think you're going so fast, I think that we're going to break all records in terms of numbers of pages of transcript. We have to check whether the city commander of Vukovar testified here under a pseudonym, because if that is the case, we will have to redact. Because everyone can know who it is, especially since in the Mrkic judgement, his name appears.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] [Previous translation continues]... Mr. President. Mr. President, nobody knows who that is. You can take a poll. Nobody knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the commander of the city of Vukovar, during the liberation of Vukovar, it is an open secret. It's in the judgement of the Mrkic case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nobody knows who that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the Legal Officer will double-check on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Paragraph 66 says: "Still, with regard to Ovcara, I had stories that the Arkan's Men took some Croats there and executed them. In informal conversations with volunteers, I heard nothing about the alleged involvement of Kameni or other volunteers in Ovcara events." Did you really hear that Arkan's men killed Croats there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Set aside the fact that we know that Arkan's men did commit crimes in other locations, they were simply not present in Ovcara; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it true that they were not present at all in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in Sector South.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They were in Sector North, under the command of the Novi Sad Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And they could have appeared in Sector South only after the fighting was over in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But nobody ever heard that Arkan's men were killing in Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Were you in Zvornik in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Mali Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But not to Veliki Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In paragraph 67, we read that you heard that some civilians had been killed in Vocin, and "I was informed about it through the volunteers." Then paragraph 68: "White Eagles were there, and after that we accused each other, Bokan, the commander of White Eagles and we in the staff of the Radical Party, we accused each other of these crimes." Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The truth is I read in enemy papers, and we know what enemy newspapers are, what they wrote about Vocin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: However, we know about it because I published all my public speeches, in my books. We condemned this crime, and we blamed the White Eagles.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We didn't mention Bokan. I don't know that he was involved to this day. However, Bokan never claimed that it was the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party who had done it. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From all I know, it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You mean what I'm saying is true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Then how come your statement says that we accused each other?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In paragraph 57, it says that you -- sorry, 67, it says that you went to tour Arkan's training centre in Erdut.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said. I said in the summer of 1991, I dropped by at Erdut because I had a friend who was in Arkan's unit and I wanted to bring him over to our unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that I was there once, that I passed through, I had a look at the centre, and then went on to Borovo Selo? Why would that be strange?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not strange.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Because the commander of Baranja of Western Slavonia and Srem was Badza; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And I saw Arkan, what does it mean? If I met him there and then at a funeral, and at the session of the National Assembly in 1993, does that mean that we co-operated?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that cannot mean that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that already in the 1980s I was in contact with Arkan?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were conflicts between you even before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What if I tell you that a witness stated here that Arkan had come to Zvornik in a police car of the Federal Ministry of the Interior with those rotating lights on the roof; would you be surprised?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in the least.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you know that Arkan worked for the Federal Ministry of the Interior for years?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It also says here that we collaborated and co-ordinated activities with Arkan, although we acted separately. Did you state that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand. You have to repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Here is what it says: "Let me clarify. We acted separately, but we collaborated and co-ordinated our activities with Arkan. Therefore, it was normal to me to go and see Arkan, not to duplicate our presence on the ground. Ljubisa Petkovic had contacts with Arkan for the same reasons." However, you never saw Arkan in the War Staff. What were we supposed to co-ordinate with him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that. What I said was this: It happened that our units and Arkan's units happened to be in the same area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That was in Tenja, but also in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know how many fighters Arkan had in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A small number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Thirty-nine. And do you know that his -- that the War Staff of Zvornik -- or, rather, the Crisis Staff paid him to get involved in the fighting in Zvornik, that he was not under the control of the JNA? I presented a statement of Colonel Tacic, who demanded that Arkan be removed from Zvornik urgently. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Further on, it says in paragraph 72: "Seselj did not have a good relationship with Arkan, although they co-operated in field activities." Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that you were not in a good relationship with Arkan, but it did happen that his and our unit shared the same area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How could we co-operate on the ground, in what possible way?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were under the command of the Territorial Defence, which means that we could not co-operate with anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So how could I co-operate with him on the ground?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm really not clear on that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It says that Goran Hadzic came to the War Staff, as well as Milan Matic. When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They came to me, but not to the War Staff. What would their business in the War Staff be?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Milan Martic did come, but I don't remember Goran Hadzic. Did Goran Hadzic ever come? I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So how come it's in paragraph 72 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that somebody found this suitable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Paragraph 73, Milan Babic, you didn't see him at the War Staff, but it says that I and Babic were in conflict. Where did we conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said later on, with regard to the Babic and Martic elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: First of all, let me say that there was no conflict between me and Martic until the end of 1993.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say later, when Martic was elected president.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let me jog your memory. In the 1993 elections in Republic of Serbian Krajina, those were presidential elections, we Radicals had our own candidate, Drago Leskovac?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And there were also Milan Babic and Martic who ran, and they went into the second round. And do you remember that in the second round we supported Milan Babic against Martic? Were we in conflict with Martic? Do you remember that Martic attacked me when I conflicted with Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really forget those details.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that at the beginning of 1994, Babic arrived in Belgrade to agree a coalition with the Radicals? We held a press conference together at the Tanjug Press Centre. That was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1994, I was not involved in any of the political matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You could watch that on TV. And then Babic agreed coalition with Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Borislav Nikolic, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So that was the original -- our conflict, from 1994, when he went back on our coalition. I did not have any other conflict with Babic before he came to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mean the political conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When he came to The Hague and made a deal with the OTP, we conflicted, and he ran away from me. That's the only truth about that. In paragraph 74, it says: "Most of the requests for volunteers for the area of Eastern Slavonia came from Milan Lancuzanin, also known as Kameni, who was also a member of the SRS, and he was our contact there." Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No way. Milan Lancuzanin was a member of the SDS. It was only later that he became a member of the SRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Only when the war was over?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that we sent volunteers to Vukovar in agreement with the JNA and in no other way?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 1st of October and thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that high-ranking officers of the JNA arrived in the headquarters of the SRS?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that Ljubisa Petkovic went directly to the General Staff in order to agree on things with General Ljubomir Domazetovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What was General Domazetovic? Was he the deputy of the secretary-general, the deputy of the chief of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The deputy of the chief of General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I believe you're right. In paragraph 75, it says that the government of SBWS decided to deploy our units in Dalj, which was held by Goran Hadzic, and that you went twice to the Arkan's training centre in Erdut. Why would SRS volunteers be deployed in Dalj? There was no threat against Dalj at that time. Dalj had been liberated, and there was no threat after that.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That had nothing whatsoever to do with what I actually stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So this is not your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This doesn't make sense. Why would you send volunteers to Dalj, a place that liberated amongst -- very early on amongst the first ones to be liberated?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I agree with you. In paragraph 77, it says that you allegedly stated: "In relation to the contacts between the War Staff of the SRS and the representatives of the State Security of Serbia, I can say that I was introduced to a person called Branko Stanisic, if that was his real name at all. He came together with Ljubisa Petkovic to the War Staff. On one occasion, Petkovic and I went to see him, to his office at the SUP office at Stari Grad. The reason for the meeting was that Petkovic needed to resolve some administrative issues regarding volunteers, but I don't know what the topic was, because the meeting regarding that was cancelled and was held at a later stage. I would like to add that that same person, Branko Stanisic, alleged being a distant cousin of Jovica Stanisic." Did you state this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that he -- in prison, I shared the same block with Jovica Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Jovica Stanisic says that he never heard of that Stanisic, Branko Stanisic, and that they cannot be related. Do you believe him?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljubisa Petkovic was here. He would be best suited to tell you who that person is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Jovica Stanisic wants to take me to court because I published some confidential documents, and there's no reason for him to state anything against me. What would be the link between the State Security of Serbia and an official who had his office in Stari Grad? Was that the headquarters of UDBA?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no way. Maybe Ljubisa had something private, some private matter to deal with there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. Paragraph 78, you speak about conflicts between volunteers and police. That's true. Our volunteers used to -- policemen, Communists, and they called them Chetniks, but those conflicts all happened before the 1st of October?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When our volunteers went there in civilian clothes, without weapons, and when the police officers tried to prevent that, they couldn't arrest them because they didn't have either weapons or uniforms --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the OTP to conduct a quick research and see whether the commander of Mostar, after the month of November, was granted protective measures, because I have a question mark in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, do you mean Mostar or something else? In the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vukovar. I'm sorry, Vukovar. And I would like to know whether this person, the commander of the town of Vukovar, after it fell, had been given protective measures. The Legal Officer is giving me a name, but I have a problem with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think it would speed up the process considerably if maybe we went into private session and the accused could give us the name. Then it's easier for us to do our research. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not going to tell you anything in private session, nothing. I will keep quiet, I will not say a word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... redact the relevant part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall temporarily redact page 93, which mentions the commander of the town of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour -- [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can redact the transcript as much as you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] We will make an effort to get back to the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll have to find medicine against attempts to threaten the public nature of these proceedings. I don't know what the medicine will be, but there must be something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Paragraph 78, you say that the War Staff of the SRS co-operated with the State Security of Serbia, in terms of co-ordination. What co-ordination? What could we have co-ordinated with them in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What comes to mind is a remedy, and that would be for the Trial Chamber to prohibit the broadcasting of this on Serbian Television. This would be a good form of medicine. This is something that just comes to mind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be a fantastic remedy, Mr. President. Why didn't you think of that three years ago? You would have been so much more successful. You would have finished these proceedings two years and eleven months ago. Now it's a bit late, I believe. I'm not trying to spite you, but you seem to be trying to spite me. I don't know why. Are you bothered because I'm defending myself and doing so very successfully? I believe that this is the main problem here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And it says: "As far as I know, we did not have any volunteers under the command of the State Security of Serbia. In any case, there was co-operation at all levels. We co-ordinated our work with everybody who was present on the ground, the army, the TO, Arkan, the police. I don't have any information about possible contacts between Seselj and Jovica Stanisic and/or Franko Simatovic. It is possible that Seselj went to see them, but not the other way around." What does all this mean in your alleged statement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't a clue. I've never heard of this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You're not even aware of the fact that this entered your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is preposterous. Not only did I not know, this is ridiculous. It has nothing whatsoever to do with the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you believe me if I tell you that I was never in the main office of the State Security?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any reason not to believe you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, I was in the Federal State Security when Mihajl Kertes was appointed its boss. Brano Crncevic was present, and Kertes gave me a pistol on that occasion, a CZ-99, which I later on registered into my name. I was there once, and I was never in Jovica Stanisic's office. Do you believe me when I say that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Which doesn't mean that I didn't know him. I met him in November 1992. In paragraph 79, it says that you allegedly stated: "When our volunteers --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Mr. Seselj has just said -- I shall be very brief. I do my work as a Judge. When I see incriminating or non-incriminating evidence, I always step in. He has just said that he met Stanisic in November 1992. According to the indictment, the joint criminal enterprise goes back to 1991. So the Prosecutor states that Stanisic knew Mr. Seselj in 1991, already. If he knew him in November 1992, then we have a problem. As far as you know, Mr. Seselj got to know Mr. Stanisic at what point in time? Perhaps you don't know. If you don't know, please tell me. If you do know, tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't even know that the two of them were in contact at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't know. Just one other question. I put questions which seem to me to be essential, and I avoid wasting any time. Mr. Seselj testified in the Milosevic case and implicated your neighbour, and he said that Mr. Petkovic had been infiltrated into the Serbian Radical Party by the Ministry of the Interior, by the MUP, the State Services. What do you think of this, since you know Mr. Petkovic well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know Mr. Petkovic rather well, but whether he was infiltrated in the Serbian Radical Party or not, I wouldn't know. Mr. Seselj would probably be able to answer your question much better than I can.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you misinterpreted my testimony in the Milosevic case. I didn't say that he had infiltrated -- been infiltrated by the service. We suspected Ljubisa Petkovic in 1993, that he started working for that service at that time. In terms of partisan questions, that's my testimony in the Milosevic case, and that's when Ljubisa Petkovic was expelled from the party. But he was rehabilitated later on. He's heroic [indiscernible] primarily before The Hague Tribunal, and this is a -- a party matter, and this is my testimony in the Milosevic case, and you are more than welcome to check all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, we will check. Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'm asking for a simple clarification. It wasn't captured in the English transcript. The name that Mr. Seselj gave, forgive me if I mispronounce it, but if he could say it again so that it can be captured. I believe it was Brana Crncevic, but it didn't make its way into the transcript. So if he could perhaps repeat the name.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Novelist Brana Crncevic was in Kertes' office. For a while, he was the head of the State Security Service, and on that occasion Kertes [realtime transcript read in error "Crncevic"] gave me a pistol, CZ-99, with two rounds of ammunition. And that was in 1992, sometime in June or July. I can't remember exactly when. Mr. President, if you're interested, I'd like to remind you that I described my first encounter with Jovica Stanisic at Jovica Stanisic's request in November 1992. He was waiting for me in a car in front of the National Assembly. I entered his car, and he informed me that an assassination was being prepared by Brano Micinic [as interpreted], also known as Montenegrin Arkan, in Montenegro, on the eve of my travel to Montenegro as part of my campaign, and I never saw Mr. Stanisic before that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If I may, again a little transcript issue. On page 106, line 23 -- 22, it says: "On that occasion, Crncevic gave me a pistol." I believe it was Kertes that gave the accused --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript is not correct. Kertes gave me the pistol, and Crncevic was only there. I found him there in Kertes' office, the two of them in a conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Brana Crncevic is famous for socialising with the secret police, and that's probably why he was there. I didn't, myself, associate with the secret police, but sometimes from time to time I would bump into them in one way or another. We have now arrived at paragraph 79, in which you allegedly said: "Whenever our volunteers were transferred to the front-line in Bosnia, there was never a problem. I had with me a document that consisted of three or more A4 separate pages. And one would be the TO request from the field signed by the local TO commander. The second would be the approval or decision of the War Staff signed by ..." And so on and so forth. How come -- since from December 1991 you were not a member of the War Staff, why is that in your statement, since you were not a member of the War Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could I have done this, since I had resigned in September [as interpreted] of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I know that he didn't, but how come it's in part of your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a question for me, but for the person who typed this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The statement was typed by The Hague investigators.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You signed first the statement in English and then, by initial, you signed the third one in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you give me the time that Mr. Seselj has used so that I can be informed of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you have 15 minutes left. You have had one hour and 45 minutes so far. As you know, Ms. Biersay has more than 30 minutes to put extra questions. So since you wanted to have the last word, you can stop now and give the floor back to Ms. Biersay, or use up your 15 minutes. You may choose.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said I had a little over 15 minutes; right? Let me just ask one more question, and then I'll be finished with the first statement. No, I'd rather use all my time. I had to fight for the right to have the last word after the Prosecution, but I don't have to exercise that right all the time. Let me finish with this -- use up all my time, and then Ms. Biersay can ask whatever she likes, because I'd like to go through the second statement as well; whereas the third, fourth, and fifth are mainly repetition, with a number of corrections. Let me finish this. I don't care what Ms. Biersay is going to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 83, it says that: "JNA uniforms were issued to us in the Vasa Carapic Barracks in Belgrade in the vicinity of the Military Medical Academy." Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that on one occasion, we got uniforms at that barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What it says here, every time you got them there, and one or two batches in Bubanj Potok. I never heard of a single group got any uniforms at barracks. I know that all groups received them at Bubanj Potok. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I personally led one group to Slavonia, and they got their uniforms at the barracks Vasa Carapic, but that was once.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So it's not true that it was every time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you got mainly your uniforms from the Bubanj Potok barracks and only once in the Vasa Carapic Barracks in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That I can believe, but it's certainly cannot not true, what it says there. Then it says that in the end of June or early July, you resigned from the War Staff and the Serbian Chetnik Movement. It's not true, is it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it's not true. You know that. You have the paper in front of you. I never abandoned the Serbian Chetnik Movement before it ceased to exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So how did this come to be written in your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not a question for me, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It must have suited them; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let's see your statement from January 2004. Some things are typical. In paragraph 11, you allegedly described the members of the Central Homeland Administration of the Serbian Chetnik Movement, and among others, you enumerate some people who were really there, including me. You mentioned Stanoje Djordjevic as vice-president, then Maja Gojkovic, Jovan Glamocanin, Novak Savic, Nikola Poplasen, and so on. Were they ever members of the Serbian Chetnik Movement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them were never in the Serbian Chetnik Movement. They were later members of the Central Homeland Administration, but much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In paragraph 12, Rado Leskovac joined later, it says. Was he ever a member of the Serbian Chetnik Movement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They must have confused it with the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember what I'm going to say to you now? The Central Administration was in the Serbian Chetnik Movement, whereas the Serbian Radical Party was set up later and it had a main board, and it had a main board for a long time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And we abolished that section in 1994?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And we changed the statute in 1996. We, in the Radical Party, introduced the Central Homeland Administration to replace the main board; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let's clear these matters, because what we read here is improbable. Then in paragraph 15, you say that the Crisis Staff changed its name into War Staff on the 1st of September. Yesterday, you said 1st October, and that's the truth?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As soon as the imminent threat of war was proclaimed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How does "1st September" appear here?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know better.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We both know better, but that's what it says here. Do you have any idea how many Geneva Conventions there are?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant the 1948 Geneva Convention.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: "Geneva Conventions" is a plural. Do you know how many there are?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant the rules of the Geneva Convention in 1948.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you served in the army, you did your military service. Did all of us who served in the army, in a subject called "All People's Defence" for all arms and services, didn't we all learn how to treat prisoners of war and civilians?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Everybody who did their compulsory military service had to be perfectly clear about the fact that prisoners of war, women, children, and civilians, must not be mistreated or tortured, that they must be provided with decent living conditions.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did learn that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Didn't all of us who served in the army know that no harm must be done to civilians, prisoners of war, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So nobody who committed crimes in this war can justify themselves by saying they did not know what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: At one point here, you mention that we were sending volunteers to Visegrad. Did we ever send volunteers to Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm skipping paragraphs. It says somewhere else that you claimed that Milan Lukic was a member of the Serbian Radical Party. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's ridiculous. I heard of Milan Lukic only after that incident in Strpci, after the war, when the trial began.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In paragraph 85, it says that you allegedly said: "I heard that a man called Milan Lukic commanded a volunteer unit of the SRS in Visegrad, but I don't know anything about him or his activities. His name began to appear frequently in the media after he was kidnapped by the Muslims, but before that I never heard about him."

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Abducted by the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's what it says here. And as far as I know, he was not a member of the SRS in 1992. Do you know that Milan Lukic was convicted to life imprisonment here?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He's in the same cell block as I. He was convicted for several crimes that were ascribed to him, but the two most horrendous crimes were completely fabricated. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was convicted for burning 70 civilians in a house in Pionirska Street and another 70 civilians in a house in Bikovac. US experts came to The Hague Tribunal and confirmed that there is no trace of any fire whatsoever in these houses, let alone of people being burned. Many of these alleged victims have been determined to still be alive. Have you ever heard about this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but anything is possible here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He is notorious in the Serbian public and further afield, and do you know that he was paid damages for 14 months that he spent in prison?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was tried in absentia for the Severin incident, but the two most heinous crimes for which he was tried here were a complete fabrication. Nobody ever heard of them. Now, you were very involved in the war, first directly, and later on you followed the situation very closely. Did anyone ever hear that in Visegrad, in two separate houses, in two separate incidents, burnt 70 civilians each time? It's such a horrendous piece of news that nobody could ever forget it.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard about that in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was the OTP clearly tendentious in trying to link me in some way to Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They must have had intentions, but they didn't manage?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In paragraph 57, I see they tried to link me with Goran Jelasic, but it says here you said you didn't know the name at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Mr. Seselj, in paragraph 57, is going to put a question to you, but I have a question to put to you regarding paragraph 31. In paragraph 31, there is something that -- some material evidence. For a reasonable trier of fact, it would be easy to see whether you're lying or not or whether it's the Prosecutor who included sentences in this statement that you did not say. In paragraph 31, it says that in April 1992, at the offices of the Serbian Radical Party, you received a fax coming from the municipality -- the Serbian municipality of Zvornik in order for volunteers to be sent. This is material evidence which can be easily checked if we have access to the telephone exchange and check whether a fax was sent on that day, on the 2nd or on the 3rd of April. However, you said to us earlier on that you actually left those offices in December 1991, so you could not be there in April 1992, unless you are lying. And if you were not there, then obviously you could not have received the fax there. So it's either you or whoever drafted this document who is lying, because there is major material evidence here. So what are you saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm stating here, under oath, that I submitted my resignation in December 1991. Thus, in April 1992, I could not have received any fax message, nor did I have any duties or responsibilities in the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, to conclude, you have three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It says here that: "Branislav Vakic and Oliver Dennis Barrett commanded our volunteers in Herzegovina." Right, that's true?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I know it's a fact. So it surprises me to read that Oliver Barrett is of Jewish origin. Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that the Chetnik vojvoda, late Oliver Dennis Barrett, was Albanian, his real name was Mujo Bunjaku; never heard of that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cant' remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now something for dessert. The Presiding Judge Antonetti asked you about our programme, the platform of the Serbian Chetnik Movement, the idea to move out 360.000 ethnic Albanians who had driven out Serbs from Kosovo when they moved in during the Ottoman occupation. Now, he asked, Were the Serbs supposed to return to Serbia, like Albanians were supposed to return to Albania? Do you understand that during the fascist occupation, the Nazi occupation, those Albanians were forcibly moved into Kosovo and settled in properties on land from which Serbs were driven out?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know, and I know that Tito's regime forbade the Serbs, after the war, to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you also know that Serbs were not forcibly resettled in Slavonia and Dalmatia and other areas in Croatia; instead, the Austrian emperor invited them to settle there when the Austrians drove out the Ottoman Turks away from Vienna, and conquered these areas, Lika, Vojvodina, Baranja, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were there to protect the borders of the Austrian Empire.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, and also because Croatians fled from the Ottoman occupation, and the Serbs were settled in vacant properties.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There was a border area created where Serbs were relieved from taxes and their only duty was to fight for the Austrian Empire.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the military krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that this military krajina was annexed to Croatia, with the consent of the Serbs, on the condition that Serbs be on equal footing with the Croatians as a constituent nation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So Serbs could not leave their homes. They had been settled there in empty land. They had not driven Croats, like Serbs were driven out by Albanians?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: However, the new Ustasha regime of Franjo Tudjman drove out all the Serbs from the western areas of Croatia in 1995.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN RANKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We know that after Operations Flash and Storm.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any more time, do I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you have by far gone over the two-hour limit, and I did not deduct the 30 seconds that I was planning to deduct from your two hours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My sincere thanks, Mr. President. Although you can't believe me when I say it's sincere, but it's sincere this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Ms. Biersay, you have some time left. If you have additional questions, please do so now.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity, Your Honour. At this time, we have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think that the interpreters would be very thankful to you. Witness, on behalf of my colleague -- Judge Harhoff had to leave, so he asked me to apologise on his behalf. But on behalf of all my colleagues, we would like to thank you for having come, upon the request of the Trial Chamber, and we are wishing you all the best in the building industry, from what I believed. I'm going to ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I said that it would probably be the last witness before the 98 bis, but there is one slight uncertainty regarding two witnesses because we are doing some medical checks to see what's their state of health, and I think that we will have some answer soon. And in that case, we will not have any more witnesses. And as I mentioned yesterday, there are several motions that have been filed, but you said you would not reply to those motions. This being said, the Chamber has to hand down some decisions, including regarding the judicial notice as well as the motions regarding your speeches, your statements before the General Assembly -- the National Assembly, so we're going to have to look at this. But we will not be able to hand down any decision within the next 24 hours. We may be able to meet again for an administrative hearing in order to take stock of the situation, and, if required, you could raise some new issues. There might be some; one never knows. And as soon as we will be able to, we will issue a scheduling order for this 98 bis procedure. Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have to correct you ever so slightly. In principle, I am in favour of admission, but anything that I say in the courtroom or any of my interviews should be identified. I should be allowed to comment like we did with the video-clips. If you admit all these documents without that, this will constitute a breach of my constitutional right. No single document can or may be admitted if it is not on the record. The Prosecution should say why they're tendering the document, and I should be heard on whether I agree or whether I disagree with the admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are perfectly right, but I do not have the motion from the Prosecutor before me. But I believe that, document by document, it must have stated the relevance and it must have quoted the paragraphs of the indictment, and this motion must also state what is incriminating. And during the course of this procedure, you can go through this and you can challenge formally the fact that the Prosecutor attaches one of your speeches or one of your sentences to one paragraph of the indictment, and you can put that in writing. This is why I said yesterday that it's going to take time. I will personally have to sort out everything in chronological order. I will have to look into this. And I did that already, and it took me five hours just for that. So this involves a great deal of work. I realise that you are not getting any help. We're not going to dwell on this. But this is something that could be very useful for us, because you are in the best position to tell us that the speech meant this and not what the Prosecutor was saying, it has nothing to do with the indictment, and so on and so forth. And this is what is important here. If you're not saying anything, the Trial Chamber will look at it and they will say, Well, indeed, there is a link between this and the indictment, and there will be a decision on admitting this. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Less than half a minute. Mr. President, if this was a civil proceedings, that could be the case. But this is a criminal case, and the principle of admission in court has to be respected, the principal of orality of the procedure, and I insist on that. If you do not respect that, what can I do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, do you have something to say before we free our interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Very briefly, now that we're on the motion. Sort of a very technical minor thing, but we filed the motion as an annex to a motion for an extension of the page limit. I'm assuming that we can just take it that now that Your Honours have granted the extension of the pages, we don't need to re-file the motion, we can just consider the annex as the motion and proceed on that basis. That's the only thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, because we granted you this extension. So we will set up the date for an administrative hearing, and by then I will be in a position to tell you what has been the decision of the Trial Chamber as for the last two witnesses. And I thank you very much, and I wish you a very good evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: 7.15 p.m., sine die.
